scenes.title: Friday night
scenes.text: On Friday night, September twenty-sixth, twenty twenty-five, a fire broke out in a government data center in Day-jun, South Korea. Across the country, public services began to go dark.

scenes.title: Batteries on the move
scenes.text: It began in a fifth-floor server room, where lithium-ion batteries were being moved to the basement. Sparks, then smoke, then flames. Why it happened was still under investigation.

scenes.title: 647 systems, one building
scenes.text: The building ran six hundred and forty-seven government systems. Ninety-six were burned. The other five hundred and fifty-one were shut down before the heat could reach them. Government websites, Korea Post and the mobile I-D app all went offline.

scenes.title: The drive with no copy
scenes.text: Most systems had daily backups, including a copy at a remote site. One did not. Gee Drive, where civil servants had stored their work since twenty eighteen, held about eight hundred and fifty-eight terabytes. Officials said its design allowed no outside copy. When the room burned, it was gone.

scenes.title: Weeks to come back
scenes.text: The rest came back slowly. Six days later, seventeen percent. By the end of October, eighty-nine. Forty-nine days after the fire, ninety-eight. But Gee Drive's files could only be rebuilt from emails, personal computers and paper.

scenes.title: A copy somewhere else
scenes.text: Police booked four people on suspicion of negligence. A booking is not a verdict. The lesson is older than any data center: a backup is a copy somewhere else.
